narrative_idea_gen: Told entirely through intercepted telegrams, scathing letters to territorial newspapers, passive-aggressive minutes from weekly meetings, and one postmaster's increasingly exasperated marginal annotations, this is the story of the Burnished Rose Ornithological Society of Lark Creek, Wyoming Territory, 1881—five fiercely opinionated amateur birdwatchers from violently different walks of life (a disgraced Boston debutante, a newly freed Black cowhand, a ex-Pinkerton with a drinking problem, a Chinese railroad surveyor, and the outlaw queen of a defunct gang) who are forced by a federal land office clerical error into joint stewardship of the same 200-acre parcel, and who discover that the only way to prevent a copper mining company from seizing it is to maintain its official designation as a "scientific society claim." The postmaster, Elwin Briggs—who handles every piece of their correspondence and thus sees the full picture none of them individually possesses—narrates the margins with omniscient weariness as their escalating war of devastating wit, elaborate social one-upmanship, and ruthlessly polite insults slowly, accidentally forges them into a genuine fellowship, even as each secretly authors anonymous takedowns of the others in the *Lark Creek Clarion*'s letters column. The core tension ratchets tighter when the mining company hires a charm-offensive "naturalist" to infiltrate the group, and the only way to unmask him is for five people who communicate primarily through barbed pleasantries to actually trust each other with the truth.

# Seven Structural Beats for *The Burnished Rose Ornithological Society*

---

## Beat 1: The Clerical Error — Five Names on One Deed

**Concrete Action:** A bundle of federal land office documents arrives at the Lark Creek post office, addressed to five different individuals at five different forwarding addresses, all granting stewardship of the same 200-acre parcel. Each recipient sends a telegram of acceptance before any learns of the others. The documents themselves—filed by a clerk who apparently copied five separate applications onto one survey plat—are reproduced, followed by the five telegrams of confirmation (each revealing character through diction and telegraph economy), followed by the five telegrams of outrage when the recipients converge on the property and discover each other. Postmaster Elwin Briggs's first marginal annotation appears here, dry and already tired: a note that he processed all ten telegrams and recognized the collision before any of them did, and that he considered warning someone but "could not determine whom to disappoint, since all five seemed the type to shoot a messenger."

**Narrative Technique — Polyphonic Establishment Through Document Collision:** The equivalent of Gogol's comic-genealogical opening. Rather than introducing characters through description, the story drops five documents side by side and lets the reader triangulate identity from the bureaucratic residue each person generates. The Boston debutante's telegram is syntactically immaculate and faintly imperious. The cowhand's is terse and functional. The ex-Pinkerton's contains a misspelling that suggests dictation through whiskey. The railroad surveyor's is formally precise with an undertone of someone accustomed to having paperwork questioned. The outlaw queen's is the shortest and most confident—she has clearly filed fraudulent land claims before. The clerical error itself must feel both absurd and systemically plausible: the federal land office in 1881 was genuinely a chaos engine. Briggs's annotation establishes the structural conceit: he is the only consciousness in the story that holds all threads simultaneously, but he has no power to act on them—making him a narrator defined by omniscient impotence.

**What Must Make It Work:** The scene must accomplish five introductions and one inciting accident in a form that contains zero conventional narration. Each document voice must be distinctive enough that the reader can identify the sender within a sentence by the end of the story. The comedy of the error should carry an undercurrent of the same Gogolian predestination: these five people were never supposed to meet, and the system that brought them together is the same system that will try to destroy what they build. Briggs's first annotation must establish his voice as a specific, weary, morally alert intelligence—not a neutral frame narrator but a man who sees clearly and is perpetually ignored. The tone of the opening must promise the reader that bureaucratic absurdity will be the medium through which genuine human collision occurs. The clerical error is this story's christening: an institutional accident that determines everything.

---

## Beat 2: The First Meeting and the Establishment of Hostilities

**Concrete Action:** The minutes of the first "meeting" of the five co-stewards—taken by whoever lost the argument about who would take minutes (the surveyor, whose penmanship is noted as "mechanical and therefore trusted"). The minutes record: a forty-minute dispute over the name of the group (the debutante proposes "The Burnished Rose Ornithological Society" in a tone the minutes describe as "not open to amendment"); a near-physical altercation between the Pinkerton and the outlaw queen, who recognize each other from a previous professional encounter; the cowhand's quiet suggestion that they simply divide the parcel into five portions, which is ignored by everyone; and the surveyor's observation that none of them can actually identify a single bird native to the territory, which is received with hostility. A subsequent issue of the *Lark Creek Clarion* prints five anonymous letters to the editor, each savaging a thinly disguised version of one of the other four members. Briggs's annotation on the minutes, in red pencil: he identifies the author of each anonymous letter by matching handwriting, ink type, and the postmark timing, and notes that "each believes their contribution to the Clarion uniquely clever and wholly undetectable."

**Narrative Technique — The Ensemble as Mutual Surveillance Network:** This beat must establish the foundational dynamic: five people who see each other with devastating clarity but who are blind to how clearly they themselves are seen. The minutes—formal, supposedly objective—are in fact a deeply partisan document, because whoever records the minutes controls the narrative. The surveyor's dry, technical prose subtly editorializes through what it chooses to render verbatim versus what it summarizes. The anonymous *Clarion* letters function as a second, shadow layer of characterization: what each person chooses to attack in the others reveals what they most fear about themselves. The debutante mocks the cowhand's grammar; the cowhand mocks the debutante's uselessness; the Pinkerton mocks everyone's naivety about danger; the outlaw queen mocks everyone's pretension to lawfulness; the surveyor mocks everyone's imprecision. Briggs's marginalia become the structural glue—he is the only reader who holds both the official and anonymous documents simultaneously, and his annotations perform the work of a Greek chorus: moral commentary from someone with no power to intervene.

**What Must Make It Work:** The hostilities must be genuinely funny—these people must be world-class insulters operating under the constraint of period-appropriate politeness, which means the savagery must be conveyed through syntax, implication, and the weaponization of courtesy. But within the comedy, the reader must detect the five different shapes of loneliness and displacement that brought each person to a 200-acre parcel in Wyoming in the first place. Nobody files a land claim in Lark Creek because their life went according to plan. The beat must also introduce the *Clarion* letters as a structural motif that will pay off later: the anonymous column is the space where truth gets told in the wrong register—cruelty voicing genuine perception. And Briggs's ability to identify every author is the first signal that he understands these people better than they understand themselves or each other. His weariness is not detachment; it is the exhaustion of enforced intimacy with people he cannot reach.

---

## Beat 3: The Mining Company's First Approach and the Discovery of the Loophole

**Concrete Action:** A letter arrives from the Consolidated Lode & Copper Company of Denver, addressed to "The Proprietor(s) of Parcel 1177-C, Fremont County," offering to purchase the land at a suspiciously generous price. Simultaneously, a telegram from the territorial land office informs the stewards that their joint claim is under review due to the original filing error and will be dissolved unless the parcel's official designation—"Scientific Society Claim"—is actively maintained through documented evidence of ongoing scientific activity. The five stewards, in a flurry of cross-telegrams, each try to handle the situation independently: the debutante writes a haughty refusal to the mining company on personal stationery; the Pinkerton sends a threatening counter-letter implying he knows things about the company's operations; the outlaw queen attempts to negotiate a secret side deal; the cowhand quietly begins actually cataloging birds; and the surveyor researches the legal requirements. Meeting minutes record a second gathering, this one fractious but focused, in which they realize—through the surveyor's presentation—that the only way to keep the land is to produce quarterly ornithological reports filed with the territorial office. None of them knows what an ornithological report looks like. Briggs annotates a forwarded copy of the mining company's letter: "They do not want this land for its copper. They want it because it sits above the water table that feeds every claim in the valley. These five do not know what they are sitting on. Neither, I suspect, do they know what they are to each other."

**Narrative Technique — The Mundane Grail Revealed Through Bureaucratic Archaeology:** This is the story's true inciting incident, and like Petrovich's pronouncement about the overcoat, it must arrive as both a threat and a transfiguration. The land, which was merely a place to stand, becomes a thing worth defending. The loophole—"scientific society"—imposes a ludicrous requirement: these people must pretend to be something they are not (scientists, colleagues, an organization) in order to keep something real (their ground, their refuge). The narrative technique requires layering multiple document types in sequence: corporate correspondence (oily, formal), government telegram (terse, bureaucratic), personal cross-telegrams (panicked, contradictory), and meeting minutes (recording the moment of reluctant convergence). Each document type carries its own institutional voice, and the comedy arises from the collision of registers. Briggs's annotation here must perform its most important function yet: providing the strategic intelligence that none of the characters possesses. He sees the mining company's true motive. He understands the water table. He knows the stakes are existential, not commercial. But he is a postmaster—he reads, he annotates, he cannot act.

**What Must Make It Work:** The mining company must be established as a systemic threat, not a melodramatic villain. Like Gogol's "Person of Consequence," the company is dangerous not because it is evil but because it operates according to the logic of capital and legal procedure, which is indifferent to lives. The "scientific society" requirement must feel absurd and yet dead serious—the federal designation is the only thing between these five people and dispossession, and it depends on birdwatching. The comedy of five manifestly unqualified people trying to produce ornithological science is the engine of the middle act, but it must be underlaid with genuine stakes: this land is the last place each of them has. The cowhand who simply starts counting birds—while everyone else strategizes, threatens, and negotiates—must register as both the quietest and the most consequential act in the scene. Someone has to actually do the thing. The beat must end with reluctant, hostile, strategically motivated cooperation—no one trusts anyone, but everyone needs the claim.

---

## Beat 4: The Season of Barbed Cooperation and Secret Ornithology

**Concrete Action:** Over the course of several weeks, rendered through a montage of meeting minutes, cross-correspondence, *Clarion* letters, forwarded supply orders, and Briggs's increasingly voluminous annotations, the five stewards begin—resentfully, competitively, and with elaborate pretense that each is doing the others a favor—to build something. The debutante, who turns out to have genuine artistic training, begins producing bird illustrations of startling quality but insists on rendering each subject in dramatic Romantic poses that horrify the surveyor's empiricism. The cowhand compiles sighting logs with quiet, systematic patience. The surveyor drafts a proper methodology, complete with grid maps, but refuses to go outdoors until the Pinkerton "secures the perimeter." The Pinkerton, ostensibly providing security, begins leaving notes in the field log that are, unmistakably, poetry about hawks. The outlaw queen procures—through channels no one questions—a reference copy of Baird, Brewer, and Ridgway's *A History of North American Birds*. The anonymous *Clarion* takedowns continue, but shift in character: the insults become more specific, more knowledgeable, betraying an increasing and involuntary intimacy. The debutante's attacks on the cowhand's prose style now quote his field notes verbatim, which means she has been reading them with attention. Briggs annotates: "They have not yet noticed that their arguments have acquired the character of people who are listening to each other. This is the most dangerous phase."

**Narrative Technique — Accumulative Intimacy Through Hostile Documents:** This is the equivalent of Gogol's season of privation—the long middle passage where the object of desire (in this case, not a coat but a community) is being constructed through labor, sacrifice, and transformed habit. The technique is montage, but epistolary montage: the reader must feel weeks passing through the changing frequency, length, and emotional temperature of the documents. Early meeting minutes are curt and adversarial; later ones are longer, more detailed, with parenthetical asides that suggest people are lingering after adjournment. Supply orders reveal shared resources. Telegrams become less formal. The *Clarion* letters are the key barometer: as the anonymous insults become more granular and better-informed, they inadvertently reveal that each writer has been paying close, sustained attention to the person they are attacking. The structural trick is that intimacy enters the story disguised as hostility—no character admits to caring, but the documents betray them. Briggs's annotations during this section must shift from wry distance to something approaching invested concern. He is watching a community form through its own correspondence, and he knows, from the mining company letters he also processes, that time is running out.

**What Must Make It Work:** The reader must feel the slow, involuntary coalescence without any character acknowledging it overtly. This requires the documents themselves to encode the change through micro-shifts—a shared in-joke in the minutes, a telegram that assumes shared knowledge rather than explaining, a *Clarion* letter that accidentally defends the person it means to attack. The ornithological work must become genuinely interesting and genuinely good, because the stakes require it: these people are accidentally producing real science as a byproduct of trying to hold onto their land. Each character's contribution must reveal something they could not reveal through conventional social interaction: the debutante's artistry, the cowhand's systematic intelligence, the Pinkerton's hidden lyricism, the surveyor's longing for collaboration, the outlaw queen's resourcefulness reimagined as provision. The Pinkerton's hawk poems are the "favorite letters" of this story—the private devotion that betrays a richer inner life than anyone suspected. And the *Clarion* letters, like Gogol's colleagues dropping paper scraps on Akaky, are the ongoing cruelty that the reader must be made to enjoy before being made to reckon with.

---

narrative_story:
# THE BURNISHED ROSE ORNITHOLOGICAL SOCIETY

### Being an Annotated Collection of Documents, Telegrams, Meeting Minutes, Anonymous Correspondence, and Marginal Commentary Pertaining to Parcel 1177-C, Fremont County, Wyoming Territory, 1881–1882

*Compiled and annotated by Elwin Briggs, Postmaster, Lark Creek, W.T.*

---

## I. THE CLERICAL ERROR — FIVE NAMES ON ONE DEED

---

**UNITED STATES DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR**
**GENERAL LAND OFFICE**
**Cheyenne, Wyoming Territory**

**Certificate of Stewardship and Scientific Occupation**
*Filed Under the Act of March 3, 1879, as amended*

**No. 4,471**

BE IT KNOWN that pursuant to application received and survey completed, the following-described tract of public land is hereby granted in stewardship for purposes of scientific inquiry, conservation, and related occupation:

**PARCEL 1177-C**: Two hundred (200) acres, more or less, situated in the southwest quarter of Township 33 North, Range 99 West of the 6th Principal Meridian, Fremont County, Wyoming Territory, bounded on the north by Lark Creek, on the east by the wagon road to Casper, on the south by the ridgeline locally known as Bittern's Spine, and on the west by unmarked federal land extending to the Wind River Range foothills.

Said parcel is granted under the designation of **SCIENTIFIC SOCIETY CLAIM**, requiring quarterly demonstration of active scientific inquiry as condition of continued occupancy.

STEWARD(S) OF RECORD:

1. Miss Cecilia Farquhar Aldworth, care of Mrs. J. Pennington Curtis, 114 Beacon Street, Boston, Massachusetts
2. Mr. Jesse R. Creel, care of General Delivery, Rawlins, Wyoming Territory
3. Mr. Francis Xavier Mulvaney, care of The Continental Hotel, Room 14, Denver, Colorado
4. Mr. Arthur Emmons Vane, care of Union Pacific Railroad, Division of Survey, Omaha, Nebraska
5. Mrs. Pearl Kittredge, care of Post Office Box 7, Hole-in-the-Wall, Johnson County, Wyoming Territory

Given under my hand and the seal of the General Land Office this 14th day of April, 1881.

[Seal]

*Horace P. Dilworth*
*Deputy Clerk, Filing Division*

---

**[Annotation, in black ink, hand of E. Briggs:]** *Five names. One parcel. I have handled land office filings for eleven years and have never seen the like. The survey plat attached—which I have not reproduced here, as it is a single map bearing five application numbers in five different inks, each circling the identical acreage—tells the story plainly enough. Deputy Clerk Dilworth appears to have received five separate applications for five adjacent but distinct parcels, misread the survey coordinates on all five (or, more charitably, worked from a plat that had been drawn by a man in the grip of either whiskey or malaria), and filed a single omnibus certificate. Five separate filing fees were collected. Five separate applications were approved. One piece of land was granted, five times, to five people who have never met. I recognized the collision the moment the documents arrived. I considered warning someone. I could not determine whom to disappoint, since all five seemed the type to shoot a messenger.*

---

**WESTERN UNION TELEGRAPH COMPANY**

**Received at Lark Creek, W.T., April 29, 1881, 9:47 a.m.**

FROM: MISS C. F. ALDWORTH, BOSTON MASS
TO: GENERAL LAND OFFICE, CHEYENNE W.T.

I ACKNOWLEDGE RECEIPT OF CERTIFICATE NO 4471 AND ACCEPT THE TERMS OF STEWARDSHIP WITH GRATITUDE STOP I SHALL DEPART FOR WYOMING TERRITORY WITHIN THE FORTNIGHT STOP PLEASE CONFIRM THAT THE DWELLING ON THE PROPERTY IS HABITABLE AND THAT ARRANGEMENTS FOR A LADY TRAVELING WITHOUT COMPANION HAVE BEEN CONSIDERED STOP FURTHER PLEASE ADVISE WHETHER THE LOCAL SETTLEMENT OFFERS A LENDING LIBRARY OR COMPARABLE INSTITUTION STOP

C F ALDWORTH

---

**WESTERN UNION TELEGRAPH COMPANY**

**Received at Lark Creek, W.T., April 30, 1881, 2:12 p.m.**

FROM: J R CREEL, RAWLINS W.T.
TO: GENERAL LAND OFFICE, CHEYENNE W.T.

ACCEPT STOP WILL RIDE OUT TUESDAY STOP

J CREEL

---

**WESTERN UNION TELEGRAPH COMPANY**

**Received at Lark Creek, W.T., May 1, 1881, 11:03 a.m.**

FROM: F X MULVANEY, DENVER COLO
TO: GENERAL LAND OFFICE, CHEYENNE W.T.

RCEIVED CERTIFICATE AND ACCEPT SAME STOP HAVE EXAMINED TERMS AND FIND THEM AGREEABLE STOP WILL NOTE FOR THE RECORD THAT MY PREVIOUS PROFFESIONAL AFFILIATIONS WHICH NEED NOT BE ENUMERATED HERE QUALIFY ME AMPLY FOR ANY INVESTIGATIVE OR PROTECTIVE DUTIES THE STEWARDSHIP MAY REQUIRE STOP WILL ARRIVE BY STAGE FIRST WEEK OF MAY STOP SEND WHISKEY IF ABLE STOP

F MULVANEY

---

**[Annotation, in black ink, hand of E. Briggs:]** *"Professional affiliations which need not be enumerated." A Pinkerton man, then, or a former one—the diction of a man accustomed to writing reports for superiors he does not respect. The misspelling of "received" and "professional" is consistent with dictation: he spoke the telegram aloud to the Denver operator, likely from across a hotel bar. Note also "send whiskey if able," which is not customarily included in formal correspondence with the federal government.*

---

**WESTERN UNION TELEGRAPH COMPANY**

**Received at Lark Creek, W.T., May 1, 1881, 3:38 p.m.**

FROM: A E VANE, OMAHA NEBR
TO: GENERAL LAND OFFICE, CHEYENNE W.T.

I ACCEPT THE TERMS OF STEWARDSHIP CERTIFICATE NO 4471 PARCEL 1177-C STOP PLEASE CONFIRM THE SURVEY COORDINATES AS FILED MATCH THE PHYSICAL MARKERS ON SITE STOP I HAVE NOTED A DISCREPANCY BETWEEN THE DESCRIBED SOUTH BOUNDARY AND THE STANDARD USGS TOPOGRAPHIC REFERENCES FOR THE REGION AND WISH TO RESOLVE THIS PRIOR TO ARRIVAL STOP PLEASE ALSO CONFIRM THAT THE FILING FEE OF TWELVE DOLLARS HAS BEEN PROPERLY RECEIPTED UNDER MY APPLICATION NUMBER AND NOT CREDITED TO ANOTHER ACCOUNT STOP I HAVE ENCLOSED A STAMPED ENVELOPE FOR YOUR REPLY STOP

A E VANE

---

**[Annotation, in black ink, hand of E. Briggs:]** *He enclosed a stamped envelope in a telegram. This is a man who has had paperwork go wrong before and has developed the countermeasures of the perpetually correct. I anticipate he will be the first to notice the irregularity and the last to accept it.*

---

**WESTERN UNION TELEGRAPH COMPANY**

**Received at Lark Creek, W.T., May 2, 1881, 8:01 a.m.**

FROM: P KITTREDGE, HOLE IN THE WALL W.T.
TO: GENERAL LAND OFFICE, CHEYENNE W.T.

ACCEPTED STOP ON MY WAY STOP

P KITTREDGE

---

**[Annotation, in black ink, hand of E. Briggs:]** *Four words. Not even a courtesy "stop" after "way." The confidence of a woman who has filed land claims before—some of them, I would wager, for land she had a somewhat negotiable relationship with. I note that her forwarding address is Hole-in-the-Wall, which is less a town than a geographical condition. It is where people go when their previous addresses have become inadvisable. I processed all five acceptance telegrams. I knew. I said nothing. I have since asked myself whether this constituted a dereliction of duty or an act of mercy and have concluded it was neither: it was cowardice dressed in the uniform of professional discretion.*

---

**[The five following telegrams arrived within a span of forty-one hours, beginning May 9, 1881, when all five stewards had converged on Parcel 1177-C and discovered one another.]**

---

**WESTERN UNION TELEGRAPH COMPANY**

**Sent from Lark Creek, W.T., May 9, 1881, 1:14 p.m.**

FROM: MISS C. F. ALDWORTH, LARK CREEK W.T.
TO: GENERAL LAND OFFICE, CHEYENNE W.T.

I ARRIVED AT PARCEL 1177-C THIS MORNING TO FIND FOUR OTHER PERSONS ALREADY IN RESIDENCE OR IN THE PROCESS OF ESTABLISHING THEMSELVES UPON WHAT I WAS GIVEN CLEARLY TO UNDERSTAND WAS MY LAND STOP ONE OF THESE PERSONS IS A WOMAN OF FRANKLY DUBIOUS PROVENANCE WHO HAS STAKED A TENT IN WHAT SHE CALLS QUOTE THE GOOD SPOT UNQUOTE STOP ANOTHER IS A GENTLEMAN WHOSE BREATH SUGGESTS HE HAS BROUGHT MORE PROVISIONS FOR HIS LIVER THAN FOR HIS PERSON STOP A THIRD HAS DRIVEN SURVEY STAKES INTO THE MEADOW AS THOUGH HE MEANS TO BUILD A RAILROAD THROUGH MY WILDFLOWERS STOP THE FOURTH IS A COWBOY WHO WILL NOT LOOK ME IN THE EYE STOP I REQUIRE AN IMMEDIATE EXPLANATION AND A REMEDY STOP THIS IS NOT WHAT I WAS PROMISED STOP

C F ALDWORTH

---

**WESTERN UNION TELEGRAPH COMPANY**

**Sent from Lark Creek, W.T., May 9, 1881, 2:30 p.m.**

FROM: J R CREEL, LARK CREEK W.T.
TO: GENERAL LAND OFFICE, CHEYENNE W.T.

ERROR ON YOUR END STOP FIVE PEOPLE ONE PARCEL STOP FIX IT STOP

J CREEL

---

**WESTERN UNION TELEGRAPH COMPANY**

**Sent from Lark Creek, W.T., May 9, 1881, 4:02 p.m.**

FROM: F X MULVANEY, LARK CREEK W.T.
TO: GENERAL LAND OFFICE, CHEYENNE W.T.

I WISH TO REPORT WHAT IS EITHER A BUROCRATIC CATASTROPHE OR A DELIBERATE FRAUD STOP I ARRIVED AT THE PARCEL DESIGNATED IN MY CERTIFICATE TO FIND FOUR ADDITIONAL CLAIMANTS IN POSSESSION STOP ONE OF THESE CLAIMANTS I RECONIZE FROM MY PREVIOUS LINE OF WORK AND I WILL STATE PLAINLY THAT HER PRESENCE ON A FEDERAL LAND GRANT RAISES QUESTIONS I AM PROFESSIONALLY INCLINED TO PURSUE STOP I EXPECT A FULL INVESTIGATION AND I EXPECT IT YESTERDAY STOP

F MULVANEY

---

**WESTERN UNION TELEGRAPH COMPANY**

**Sent from Lark Creek, W.T., May 10, 1881, 7:15 a.m.**

FROM: A E VANE, LARK CREEK W.T.
TO: GENERAL LAND OFFICE, CHEYENNE W.T.

RE CERTIFICATE NO 4471 STOP I HAVE NOW EXAMINED THE ORIGINAL SURVEY PLAT AND CAN CONFIRM THAT THE DISCREPANCY I IDENTIFIED IN MY PREVIOUS TELEGRAM WAS NOT AN ERROR OF SURVEYING BUT AN ERROR OF FILING STOP FIVE SEPARATE APPLICATIONS HAVE BEEN MERGED ONTO A SINGLE PLAT STOP THE HANDWRITING CHANGES INK COLOR THREE TIMES IN THE SPACE OF ONE LEGAL DESCRIPTION STOP I HAVE PREPARED A DETAILED MEMORANDUM OF THE ERRORS WHICH I WILL FORWARD UNDER SEPARATE COVER STOP I AM ALSO FILING A FORMAL COMPLAINT WITH THE TERRITORIAL SURVEYOR GENERAL AND THE DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR STOP I TAKE NO PLEASURE IN THIS BUT ACCURACY MUST BE SERVED STOP

A E VANE

---

**WESTERN UNION TELEGRAPH COMPANY**

**Sent from Lark Creek, W.T., May 10, 1881, 8:44 a.m.**

FROM: P KITTREDGE, LARK CREEK W.T.
TO: GENERAL LAND OFFICE, CHEYENNE W.T.

HOW MANY TIMES DID YOU SELL THIS LAND STOP

P KITTREDGE

---

**[Annotation, in black ink, hand of E. Briggs:]** *I processed all ten telegrams—five in, five out—inside of twelve days. The outgoing five cost me more in conscience than the office earned in fees. I watched each of them compose their complaint at the counter, each certain that theirs was the rightful claim and that the others were interlopers, squatters, or worse. Miss Aldworth wrote hers standing, with gloves on. Creel wrote his in pencil on the back of a feed receipt. Mulvaney dictated his while pacing and twice changed "fraud" to a stronger word I declined to transmit. Vane arrived with his telegram pre-written, cross-referenced, and annotated with footnotes that do not reproduce in telegraph format. Mrs. Kittredge wrote hers in nine seconds, smiled at me, and left a nickel tip. They have not yet spoken to each other in any productive sense. They have, I understand, divided the single standing cabin into territories demarcated by rope and bedsheets. I give it a week before blood or before something stranger.*

---

---

Lost & Found in Osaka

Slice of Life / Coming-of-Age: First Connection. Write one scene within a larger story set in Osaka, Japan. A shy, introverted teenager & synthesizer nerd, is browsing the electronics district of Den Den Town. She is drawn to the sound of an electric guitar. A girl, slightly older and radiating confidence, is busking near the entrance to a crowded arcade, playing a blistering rendition of a classic anime theme. The scene takes us through their initial awkward interaction, transitioning into a surprisingly easy conversation. The busker, intrigued by the teenager's quiet intensity and knowledge of music, suggests they grab some sushi at a nearby kaitenzushi (conveyor belt sushi) restaurant. The teenager wears oversized headphones that keep slipping whenever she nods nervously. Write primarily in dialogue, capturing the distinct voices of the two characters: the teenager's hesitant and -- initially -- awkward speech, and the busker's more outgoing and playful tone. 
1000 words.
